firm-policy-oct6.commentDraft:
Yes. On Airbnb's Firm policy, for a stay under 28 nights:
• Cancel 30+ days before check-in: full refund
• Cancel between 7 and 30 days before: 50% refund, and you're paid 50% of the nights
• Cancel less than 7 days before: no refund on the nights, and you're paid in full

So if they cancel now, while check-in is still more than 7 days away, they'd get 50% back. Once it's inside 7 days, you keep the full amount.

You're within your rights to decline the change. One thing to weigh, though: if they cancel, you get 50% and empty nights to refill at short notice. Accepting November (at your November rate) keeps the whole booking and usually earns a good review. Depends which matters more for those dates.

It's in Airbnb's Help Centre under cancellation policies for your listing.

ltd-quickbooks-oct6.commentDraft:
Your accountant's right that software is cheaper than paying them to sort receipts by hand. But for one property there's a cheaper route than QuickBooks.

QuickBooks is around £16 a month for Simple Start or £33 for Essentials, plus VAT, though they often run first-months discounts.

The free option: open a Mettle business account (it's NatWest's, free, and works for limited companies with up to two owners). It comes with FreeAgent accounting software free, as long as you make at least one transaction a month from the account. You snap receipts into the app and it matches them to bank transactions.

Two things before you choose:
• Ask your accountant which software they work with. Some get QuickBooks or Xero at a discount for clients, which can close the gap.
• Let them decide which refurb costs are repairs and which are improvements. The tax treatment is different.

Either way, photograph every receipt now before they fade.

superhost-relist-oct6.commentDraft:
I work in short-let management, so for what it's worth, I'd push back on this.

If they create a new listing under their account, your 3 years of reviews don't come with it. Reviews stay with the old listing. You'd be starting from zero, and if you ever part ways with them, the new listing and everything it earns stays with them.

It isn't a limit of the software for everyone. Plenty of managers run their system on listings where they're a co-host with full access, so the listing stays yours.

I'd ask them:
• Is it their software that can't co-host, or their policy?
• If you end the contract, what happens to the listing?
• How do they plan to cover the drop in bookings while a new listing builds reviews?

Happy to message you if a second opinion on their offer would help.

p01-new-hosts.body:
Seen a few new hosts get caught out by this lately, so sharing.

Before you open your calendar, check these three:

1. Cleaning fee. Set one, or build cleaning into your nightly rate. Once a guest has booked, you can't add it on.

2. Minimum stay. A one-night stay with a full clean and laundry can cost you more than it earns. Plenty of hosts set a 2-night minimum and open single nights only to fill gaps.

3. Cancellation policy. Choose it on purpose. Strict protects your dates; flexible usually gets more bookings.

One more: price your first few weeks a little lower to get reviews in. Your first five reviews do more for the listing than anything else.

What do you wish you'd set up differently when you started?
p01-new-hosts.title: New hosts: three settings to fix before your first booking

p02-damage.body:
Most damage claims fail on evidence, not on the damage itself. What actually works:

• Photos before and after every stay. Dated, same angles each time. Without a 'before' photo it's your word against the guest's.
• Report it quickly. On Airbnb you generally need to request reimbursement within 14 days of checkout, so don't wait until the repair is done.
• Message the guest through the platform, not by phone or WhatsApp, so there's a record.
• Get a written quote or receipt for the repair or replacement.
• Stay polite. Angry messages read badly when the platform reviews the case.

And don't:
• take payment for damage off-platform
• leave a revenge review before the claim is settled
• throw the damaged item away before it's photographed

What's the worst thing you've had to claim for?
p02-damage.title: Guest damaged something? How to make the claim stick

p03-permissions.body:
These three catch people out, and they're expensive when they do.

1. Your mortgage lender. Most residential and standard buy-to-let mortgages don't allow short lets without the lender's consent. Ask, and get the answer in writing.

2. Your lease. If the property is leasehold, check for clauses banning business use or lets under a certain length. Freeholders do enforce them.

3. Your insurance. Standard home insurance usually doesn't cover paying guests, so if something happens during a stay you may not be covered. Airbnb's AirCover isn't a replacement for proper holiday let insurance.

None of these are hard to sort out. They just get skipped in the rush to get the listing live.

Did any of these catch you out?
p03-permissions.title: Three permissions hosts forget to get

p04-england-register.body:
Heads up for anyone running a short let in England.

The government has confirmed a national register for short-term lets, due to launch in March 2027. Once it's live, every short let will need to be registered, there'll be a fee, and you'll get a registration number to show on your listings.

The full detail (exact fee, penalties, what evidence you'll need) hasn't been published yet. But councils will be able to see who's letting what, so it's a good time to check the basics are in place:

• Gas safety certificate (every 12 months)
• Electrical check (EICR)
• Written fire risk assessment
• Insurance that covers paying guests
• Permission from your mortgage lender and freeholder, if they apply

None of this is new, but plenty of hosts have a gap or two. Easier to fix now than when the council asks.

Has anyone started getting ready for it?
p04-england-register.title: England: the short-let register is coming

p05-fire.body:
Since October 2023, government guidance for England and Wales has been clear: if you let a property to paying guests, you're legally responsible for fire safety and you need a fire risk assessment, written down.

It applies to small lets and single flats, not just hotels. In practice that means:

• A written fire risk assessment for the property, kept up to date
• Smoke alarms that work, tested between stays, with the checks recorded
• Clear escape routes and simple fire instructions for guests
• A carbon monoxide alarm wherever there's a gas, oil or wood burner

If you've never done one, the government guide 'Making your small paying guest accommodation safe from fire' walks you through it. Or pay an assessor.

It's the first thing an insurer will ask for if anything goes wrong.

Do you do yours yourself or use an assessor?
p05-fire.title: Fire safety: the written risk assessment

p06-certificates.body:
Two certificates every short-let host should have on file:

Gas safety certificate. If there are any gas appliances, a Gas Safe registered engineer has to check them every 12 months. This applies to holiday lets just as it does to long-term rentals.

Electrical safety check (EICR). Have the wiring inspected by a qualified electrician, normally every 5 years. In Scotland it's part of the short-let licence conditions, along with testing the appliances you provide. Elsewhere, insurers increasingly ask for it.

Put both renewal dates in your calendar now. Expired certificates are one of the most common gaps I come across.

How do you keep track of your renewal dates?
p06-certificates.title: Gas and electrics: the certificates to keep on file

p07-business-rates.body:
If you have a holiday let, it's worth checking you're on the right bill.

In England, to be assessed for business rates instead of council tax, the property has to be:
• available to let for at least 140 nights a year, and
• actually let for at least 70 nights.

A lot of small holiday lets on business rates qualify for Small Business Rate Relief, which can bring the bill right down if it's your only business property. If the property doesn't meet the test, it goes back on council tax, and some councils now charge second homes up to double.

In Wales the bar is higher: available for 252 nights and let for 182.

Keep your booking records. The Valuation Office can ask for evidence, and a calendar screenshot isn't much help a year later.

Has anyone had to prove their lettings to the VOA? How did it go?
p07-business-rates.title: Council tax or business rates? The 140/70 rule

p08-fhl-tax.body:
If your accountant hasn't raised this with you, it's worth asking.

The special tax treatment for Furnished Holiday Lets ended in April 2025. Holiday lets are now taxed much like ordinary rental property. The main changes:

• Mortgage interest is no longer deducted in full. You get a 20% tax credit instead, the same as buy-to-let landlords.
• No more capital allowances on new furniture and equipment. You claim replacement of domestic items relief instead.
• Holiday let profits no longer count as earnings for pension contributions.
• The old capital gains reliefs, like Business Asset Disposal Relief, no longer apply when you sell.

For higher-rate taxpayers with a mortgage, that can change the numbers a lot.

I'm not an accountant, so check your own situation with one. Just don't assume last year's figures still hold.

Has this changed your plans for your let?
p08-fhl-tax.title: Holiday let tax: what changed in April 2025

p09-scotland.body:
A quick one for anyone letting in Scotland.

Every short-term let in Scotland needs a licence from the council, including a single room in your own home. Letting without one is a criminal offence, and the licence comes with conditions you have to keep meeting, not just when you apply.

Where I see people slip:
• The licence number missing from one of their listings. It needs to be on all of them: Airbnb, Booking.com, your own site.
• Advertising more guests than the maximum occupancy on the licence.
• Gas, electrical and fire safety checks lapsing after the licence was granted.

In Edinburgh, two more: letting a whole property that isn't your own home normally needs planning permission as well, and the 5% visitor levy now applies to the first 5 nights of a stay (bookings made before 1 October 2025 are exempt). You collect it from the guest and pay it to the council.

What's been the trickiest part of licensing for you?
p09-scotland.title: Scottish hosts: is your licence number on every listing?

p10-london.body:
If you let a whole home in London, you can only do it for 90 nights a calendar year without planning permission.

Worth knowing:
• It's about entire homes. Letting a room while you live there doesn't count.
• Airbnb closes your calendar automatically after 90 nights. Not every platform does, and listing on several sites doesn't give you 90 nights on each. The council looks at the total.
• Stays of 90 nights or more in a row aren't counted, which is why a lot of London hosts fill the rest of the year with mid-term lets: contractors, relocations, people between homes.

Going over without permission can lead to enforcement action from the council.

How are other London hosts filling the rest of the year?
p10-london.title: London hosts: the 90-night rule

p11-wales.body:
If you have holiday accommodation in Wales, there's a new legal requirement: every provider has to register with the Welsh Revenue Authority by 31 March 2027. That covers self-catering cottages, Airbnbs, B&Bs and campsites.

The register comes ahead of the new visitor levy, a small charge per person per night that councils can choose to bring in. Not every council will, and they have to give 12 months' notice before they start charging.

While you're at it, a reminder: in Wales a holiday let needs to be available for 252 nights and actually let for 182 nights a year to be on business rates. Below that it's council tax, and councils can charge second homes a premium of up to 300%.

Has anyone registered yet? How long did it take?
p11-wales.title: Welsh hosts: register before 31 March 2027
